I'm a Computer Science and Engineering student at Kyung Hee University. I recently finished an AI internship at ROAI, a startup company that builds AI-driven motion-planning software for manufacturing robots.

My main interest is solving problems of a robot performing a specific task. I started robot manipulation with reinforcement learning. That expanded into robot motion planning, for more efficient task execution. What I like about research is finding the mathematical reason behind an algorithm, then finding a way to modify it. I also enjoy trying creative methods to solve problems.

Selected work

RoAI · Core Engine team · industrial internship

Diffusion-based motion planning on a real welding robot

RoAI's production planner is built on CuRobo. It generates a single optimized path per query. I explored diffusion instead, since it holds many valid candidate paths at once — so a shifted part or fixture doesn't force replanning from scratch.

I took Motion Planning Diffusion (Carvalho et al., IROS 2023 / T-RO 2025) off synthetic benchmark arms and onto a 4-arm Kawasaki BX200L spot-welding cell. I re-modeled the robot and gun, then decomposed the gun's non-convex geometry with VHACD to stop false collisions in its own gap. Any path from collision-sphere guidance still had to pass an exact FCL mesh check, cross-checked in PyBullet.

The welding gun's open C-throat (Kawasaki BX200L tool11–41): as one convex hull (left) it fills the gap where sheet metal actually sits; VHACD (right) keeps the gap real.

Code on GitHub — start with docs/CONTRIBUTIONS.md, where I separated my decisions from AI-assisted code

arm0's full 17-segment weld tour, collision-free, generated entirely by diffusion sampling (17/17, 8 seeds).

The entry path into a segment: arm0 moving from its retracted rest position into place for the next weld point — the same diffusion-sampled planning, just the approach rather than the tour itself.

SNU Brain Science Society Hackathon · 1st place (최우수상) · two days

A neural model of "I know" vs. "I don't know"

The hackathon's question was how the brain quickly decides "I don't know" something. We proposed CEN-CMT: memory search happens fast, in parallel, across the brain. If that search stays too uncertain, a monitoring-and-control circuit cuts it short. That's what produces a "don't know" answer, instead of an endless search. We also designed an experiment to test this: brain imaging first, to see if the theory's timing holds up. Then targeted brain stimulation, to see if that "cut it short" circuit actually causes the answer — not just correlates with it.

Receiving 1st place (최우수상) at the BCSC Idea Hackathon Workshop, July 2025.

Software Convergence Capstone Design · Kyung Hee University · one semester

Stabilizing offline-to-online RL with trajectory-level replay sampling

Advised by Prof. Seongho Bae, mentored by Daegyu Lim (Robros)

Robot manipulation data is expensive to collect live. So training often starts from a fixed offline dataset, then fine-tunes with limited online interaction. That raises a question: should replay sampling look the same in both phases? Naive answers — like always prioritizing high-reward or high-TD-error trajectories — quietly collapse behavior diversity when the data is fixed and TD-error isn't trustworthy yet.

We built on QC-FQL (Li et al., NeurIPS 2025) — action chunking added to Flow Q-Learning (Park et al., 2025) — with a two-phase replay sampler on top, in the spirit of Prioritized Experience Replay and Prioritized Trajectory Replay but reworked for this setting: cluster-uniform sampling offline, to keep every behavior mode in view, then rank-based TD-error sampling online, once the critic has real signal to work with.

The offline sampler: cluster trajectories by feature, sample a cluster uniformly, then a trajectory within it — so no single behavior mode dominates the critic's training signal.

The results also differed by task on Robomimic (MuJoCo-based manipulation benchmarks) — and the reason was revealing. On the short-horizon, dense-reward task, TD-error had already faded to near-zero by the end of offline training. That left little for online sampling to prioritize, so the combination raised max success rate by only +0.06 offline and +0.04 online. On the long-horizon, sparse-reward task, TD-error stayed meaningful much longer. Both phases had real signal to work with there, and the combination helped the most: max success rate rose +0.16 offline, +0.22 more online.

RoAI · AWS Summit 2026 booth · 2nd place, Physical AI category

Building the robot game booth for AWS Summit 2026

RoAI built a promotional game around an RB3-730es collaborative arm, separate from its core motion-planning product. The idea: let visitors plan a robot's path themselves, through play, and feel how hard the problem actually is.

I started by researching the robot's command specs and testing direct control. From there, I planned and built the end-effector and the obstacle map. Finally, I tested the full pipeline: movement commands entered on the web game, sent through AWS SQS to the real robot. The booth placed 2nd in the summit's Physical AI category.
